reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read Stephen and Genesis as one journey under two callings — an initial summons in Ur/Mesopotamia and a renewed call in Haran.

discrepancy.connective: The objection, pressed by the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, is that Acts 7:2-3 puts God's call in Mesopotamia before Haran while Genesis 12 issues it only after the family had settled in Haran.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells (Skeptic's Annotated Bible)
skeptic.work: Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Did God call Abraham before or after he moved to Haran?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/haran.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; the upstream source of this contradiction)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It seems most probable that Abraham had two calls, one in Ur, and the other in Haran. He left Ur at the first call, and came to Haran; he left Haran at the second call, and came into the promised land.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The classic 'two calls' harmonization: an Ur/Mesopotamia call (matching Stephen) and a Haran call (matching Gen 12), so both placements are true of distinct moments.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Not the words in Gen 12:1 for they were said in Haran, these in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt there, and besides, these are different from them …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill distinguishes two distinct divine speeches — the Mesopotamia words (Acts 7:3) from the Haran words (Gen 12:1) — directly resolving the before/after-Haran tension.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The text is clear that Abram's departure from Ur was prompted by God's calling (see study note on 11:28), but the event is described from Terah's perspective, in keeping with the patriarchy of ancient Near Eastern culture. … This cultural deference to the oldest male is evidently why Abram did not continue on to Canaan by himself at this time (see Acts 7:2-4).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Tyndale grants Stephen's point that the Ur departure was God's call, explaining Genesis's Terah-centered framing as cultural perspective rather than a competing chronology.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Acts 7:2
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this exact tension, arguing Abraham received two calls — one in Ur and one in Haran — so Stephen and Genesis describe successive stages of one journey rather than rival timings.
